devi ever : fx - About Skip to content NIN - 1,000,000 Bit : Legend of Fuzz Language: 简体中文 繁體中文 Čeština Nederlands English Suomi Français Deutsch Magyar Bahasa Indonesia Italiano 日本語 한국어 Polski Português (Brasil) Română Русский Español Svenska Türkçe Українська Cart · Downloads devi ever : fx - organic analog effects since 2003 - perfectly emulated digitally in 2026 - Plugins · Pedals · Archive · About · Socials · Retailers Goddess Zero Core · Soda Meiser Core · Vintage Fuzz Master Core · Zero Good Core coming soon™ coming soon™ YouTube · Instagram · BlueSky · Twitter Japan · California · Direct where it all started : 2003 the first batch of Tri Fuzzes : 2003 production in full swing : 2007 who knows what the future holds About Me I’ve been designing and building effects since 2003, back then under the name Effector 13. Before that, I ran the Guitar Pedal Archive, the earliest online databases devoted to stompboxes. Cataloguing pedals, schematics, and historical photos. I was particularly interested in Electro Harmonix and Japanese boutique effects. Their unusual designs made me want to build things that weren’t simply copies of older circuits. where it all started : 2003 I had no formal electronics training. My first design, the Krackle Fuzz, came from plugging components I got from Radio Shack into a breadboard until it made sound. I always saw myself more as a circuit bender than anything. One circuit would lead to another. The Krackle Fuzz became the Tri-Fuzz, the Beautiful Disaster, and eventually the Truly Beautiful Disaster. The Silver Crank led to the Vintage Fuzz Master. An abandoned design called the Doomsday Device produced the Torn’s Peaker and Never Drive. Effector 13 grew through the internet via word of mouth. Guitar World covered the Truly Beautiful Disaster in February 2004, less than a year after I began. Vintage Guitar followed with the Improbability Drive, and Tape Op later covered the Truly Beautiful Disaster, Soda Meiser, Hymn Strangle, and Synth Mangler. The pedals weren’t designed exclusively for guitar. They found their way onto basses, synthesizers, drum machines, vocals, and tabletop noise setups. Some had feedback loops, photo-sensitive controls, joysticks or several fuzz circuits fighting inside the same enclosure. The point was to find sounds that conventional effects were designed to prevent. That eventually led musicians like Trent Reznor and Kevin Shields to use my gear. the first batch of Tri Fuzzes : 2003 Effector 13 became devi ever : fx in 2009. The pedals have since been used by many incredible artists, including Alan Moulder, Mick Gordon, Nine Inch Nails, My Bloody Valentine, Depeche Mode, King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard, The Black Keys, Boris, Silversun Pickups, Wilco, Nels Cline, The Shins, Justin Meldal-Johnsen, Linkin Park, Anthrax, The Hives, Scissor Sisters, Nina Hagen Band, The Octopus Project, UNKLE, Michael Wandmacher, Wheatus, and ZZ Top. They have been used in shoegaze, industrial music, experimental rock, metal, electronic music and places I never anticipated when I built the original circuits. production in full swing : 2007 Making unusual effects accessible has always been part of the work. Alongside the main catalogue, I sold kits, published free schematics, and launched a $50 fuzz line at a time when boutique pedals were expensive and everyone in the industry vigilantly protected their circuits. Some even went so far as to cover them in resin, lol. I eventually expanded my message board into a home for other boutique fuzz makers. It became known as ilovefuzz.com, although it is no longer under my control. After spending time away from regular production, I relaunched devi ever : fx in 2022 and began building pedals again. who knows what the future holds In 2026, I started bringing the circuits into software. - **Archive parent:** Tri-Fuzz
- **Builder:** Devi Ever : FX
- **Catalog type:** Fuzz
- **Identity:** Devi Ever : FX Tri-Fuzz.

Devi Ever : FX's current historical account states that the builder began designing and building effects in **2003**, originally under the name **Effector 13**. The same account identifies the **first batch of Tri-Fuzz pedals as 2003** and says the Krackle Fuzz led to the Tri-Fuzz and later related designs.

The builder also states that **Effector 13 became devi ever : fx in 2009**. This is useful identity history for the archive because older Tri-Fuzz examples can appear under the Effector 13 name even though the canonical builder identity is now Devi Ever : FX.

The builder's historical account places Tri-Fuzz directly in the design lineage following Krackle Fuzz. It does not publish a complete Tri-Fuzz schematic or a production-wide component list on the page reviewed.
- **Exact circuit topology:** Not established in this pass.
- **Exact transistor/device:** Unknown.
- **Exact clipping/diode device:** Unknown.

A separate archived DIY-information compilation describes an evolutionary path of **Krackle Fuzz 2003 > Tri Fuzz > Super Tri Fuzz > Beautiful Disaster > Truly Beautiful Disaster**. Because that compilation is not the builder's current site, the archive uses it only as secondary lineage context.

The builder describes the overall design philosophy as intentionally unusual effects that seek sounds conventional effects were designed to prevent. The historical account identifies Tri-Fuzz as one of the early designs to emerge from that circuit-bending approach. The archive does not assign a more specific tonal profile without exact-model documentation.

- **First Tri-Fuzz batch:** 2003, according to the builder's historical account.
- **Builder-name transition:** Effector 13 became devi ever : fx in 2009.
- The surviving official history does not establish a complete numbered revision list or factory colorway sequence.

- **Identity:*
